opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that automated testing system is probably one of the most important investments we made, and the reason really comes down to scale and speed.

When we started working on Bing Chat, we were dealing with a fundamentally different kind of technology. With traditional AI systems, you could often enumerate the failure modes and test against a fairly well-defined set of inputs. But with a generative model like GPT-4 sitting behind a conversational interface, the space of possible inputs and outputs is essentially infinite. People can ask it anything, they can have long multi-turn conversations, and they can deliberately try to push it into bad behavior. So the question becomes: how do you actually know whether your mitigations are working?

Manual red teaming is incredibly valuable. We had a lot of people doing it, and they find things that you would never think of. But it doesn't scale, and it's slow. If you make a change to the metaprompt, or you update a classifier, or the underlying model changes, you can't go back and have a team of people re-test everything every single time. And we were iterating constantly, sometimes many times a day.

So what we built was a system where we could use the model itself to help simulate conversations. We'd take the harms we cared about, whether that's harmful content, jailbreaks, ungrounded responses, and so on, and use an AI system to play the role of the user and generate lots of conversations that probe those areas. Then we'd use another model, guided by carefully developed guidelines that we'd validated against human judgments, to evaluate whether the responses were problematic. That gave us measurement we could run over and over again.

What that unlocked was the ability to treat responsible AI like an engineering discipline. You identify the risks, you measure them, you put mitigations in place, and then you measure again to see if the mitigation actually helped, and also that it didn't regress something else. Without that measurement loop, you're kind of flying blind. You're making changes and hoping they help.

It also mattered because the product was moving so fast. We needed responsible AI to keep pace with the development, not be a bottleneck at the end. Having automated measurement meant every iteration could be checked, and the teams building the product got fast feedback.

And longer term, it's become the foundation for a lot of what we do now. The patterns we developed there, the simulated adversarial conversations, the AI-assisted evaluation, the grounding metrics, those have become things we've brought into our tooling so that customers building their own generative AI applications can do the same kind of testing. So it was important not just for Bing, but because it's really how we think everyone building these systems needs to work.

r001.rationale: It explains that repeated measurement checks whether mitigations helped or caused regressions, providing feedback on when safety controls need adjustment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the biggest shift for us with Bing Chat was realizing that you can't do responsible AI for a system like this the way we'd done it before. With earlier models, a lot of our evaluation was essentially manual red teaming and human review, and that works when the surface area is relatively narrow. But with a generative, open-ended conversational system, the space of things a user can ask and the space of things the model can produce is effectively infinite. You can't hand-review your way through that.

So the automated testing system became the thing that let us actually measure the problem. We built it so that we could take a harm category, say, jailbreaks or ungrounded content or generating harmful material, and automatically generate a large volume of adversarial conversations, run them against the system, and then use models to grade the outputs against a set of guidelines. That gives you a quantitative signal at a scale a human team could never produce, and critically, you can run it every single time something changes.

And that's really the part I think is underappreciated. These systems aren't static. The underlying model gets updated, the prompts change, the grounding and the search integration change, the mitigations change. Every one of those changes can shift the behavior in ways you didn't intend, and sometimes a fix for one problem makes a different one worse. If your only check is a manual red team exercise you do once before launch, you're blind to that. With the automated system, we could run the full suite as part of the release process and see, this change reduced jailbreak success rate by this much but caused a regression in this other area, and make a decision with real data.

The other thing it did was change how we worked with the red team. Instead of red teamers spending their time finding the same failure over and over, they'd find a new attack pattern, and we'd encode that into the automated system so it would keep getting tested going forward. So the human creativity goes into discovering new things, and the automation handles the coverage. That loop is what let us actually keep up with how fast the space was moving.

And honestly, it was a big investment, both in building the infrastructure and in getting the evaluation quality high enough that we trusted the grading. But I think it's the thing that made it possible to ship responsibly at all, and most of what we've built since has been built on top of it.

astra-6.text:
Because with a system like Bing Chat, you can’t understand how it’s going to behave just by testing a handful of examples manually. There are so many different things people can ask, and the conversation itself can take the system in unexpected directions. You need a way to test those behaviors repeatedly and at scale.

The automated testing system lets us take an issue we discover and turn it into something we can check as we improve the system. When we change the model or add a mitigation, we can ask: Did that actually address the problem? Did it introduce a different problem? And are we still giving people useful answers?

That makes it an investment in our ability to keep improving, rather than just a check before launch. You’re going to learn new things as people use the product, and you need a reliable way to turn that learning into better behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
Because with a system like Bing Chat, you’re not testing a fixed set of responses. It can have an open-ended conversation, and the risks can emerge over multiple turns. You need a way to test that systematically, rather than relying entirely on people trying examples by hand.

Human testing is still essential, particularly for discovering new failure modes. But once you find an issue, you want to turn it into a test that you can run again whenever you change the model or the safety system. That lets you ask: Did we actually fix the problem? And did that fix introduce a problem somewhere else?

So the investment is really in being able to learn and improve continuously. Automated testing gives you a much faster feedback loop and broader coverage, while allowing the human experts to focus on the things we don’t yet know how to test.
